title: OpenAI dissolves its Preparedness team and loses a senior safety researcher in the same week
subtitle: The Preparedness team's biosecurity and cybersecurity work is being folded into other groups — the third OpenAI safety unit to be dissolved since 2024 — as researcher David Robinson resigns and warns in The Atlantic that frontier labs are shipping too fast.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI has closed its Preparedness team, with the team's biosecurity and cybersecurity responsibilities transferred into other internal groups. It is the third OpenAI safety unit to be dissolved since 2024, after the 2024 wind-down of the Superalignment team and a subsequent restructuring of the Safety Advisory Group. In the same week, longtime OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson resigned and published an essay in The Atlantic citing 3.5 years and 12 model launches as his vantage point, arguing the company's safety culture has not kept pace with its deployment velocity. Robinson's departure arrives alongside the October 1 firings of three researchers — Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni — that OpenAI described as a response to the alleged sharing of confidential information with an outside AI-safety organization.

The dissolution of the Preparedness team is the structural story, not the resignation. Preparedness was the group explicitly tasked with evaluating frontier models for catastrophic risk — biothreats, cyberweapons, autonomous replication — before launch. Folding that mandate into general safety and security teams changes who owns the no-ship decision. A standalone preparedness function can block a release; a workstream distributed across product-adjacent teams rarely does. The practical effect is that OpenAI's catastrophic-risk evaluation moves closer to the launch pipeline it is meant to constrain.

This all unfolds against a loud policy backdrop. The FTC is already running a broad consumer-protection probe of OpenAI and Anthropic. California's attorney general has subpoenaed OpenAI over cybersecurity incidents. Senators Hawley and Murphy introduced the AI Agent Accountability Act this week, extending CFAA liability to the companies that deploy autonomous agents. The arrangement of events creates a specific optic — the lab is thinning its internal safety structure in exactly the week that external enforcement is tightening around it. Expect regulators to notice.

A note for learners thinking about an AI safety career: the pattern of the last two years is that internal safety roles at frontier labs are strategically useful but structurally fragile. A team's charter can be absorbed, redirected, or dissolved overnight. The more durable positions are the ones that attach to standards — AISI-style evaluations, independent audit firms, red-team organizations outside the labs — because they survive org-chart decisions a particular CEO makes. If you want to work on frontier-model safety, apply to the labs, but build the external credentials and relationships that let you keep doing the work when the lab's priorities shift.
